Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

despite preposition

also in spite of, notwithstanding, even though, against someone’s will, all the same, without my consent, against my will

classical

Mart. 13.81.1: quamvīs lāta gerat patella rhombum
Plin. NH 9.25: quamvīs occultus atque abditus

quamvīs

conjunction with the subjunctive; also with an adjective or participle alone

despite (being), however (much)

Latin has no preposition for “despite”: “despite the cold” becomes a clause, “though it is cold”, with quamvīs, quamquam or etsī, and tamen often marks the main clause. With an adjective alone, “however …”: quamvīs fertilis.

Other words

  • etsī … tamen — even though … still

    conjunction with the indicative; tamen in the main clause · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 12.53.1: etsī nihil habeō quod ad tē scrībam, scrībō tamen

  • invītus, invīta, invītum — despite someone, against someone’s will

    adjective, first and second declension; with a noun or pronoun in the ablative absolute: mē invītō, despite me · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 14.13.6: fēcisset nihilō minus mē invītō; Publil. Sent. R 26: quidquid invītō auferās; Traupman 296

    “Despite my wishes”: mē invītō, or contrā meam voluntātem. “Despite that”, “all the same”: nihilōminus (see however).

Examples

  • ego etsī nihil habeō quod ad tē scrībam, scrībō tamen quia tēcum loquī videor

    even though I have nothing to write to you, I write all the same, because I feel I am talking with youCic. Att. 12.53.1

  • quamvīs lāta gerat patella rhombum, rhombus lātior est tamen patellā

    however wide the dish that holds the turbot, the turbot is wider than the dishMart. 13.81.1–2

  • quamvīs sint sub aquā, sub aquā maledīcere temptant

    though they are under water, under water they still try to curseOv. Met. 6.376

  • ut ager quamvīs fertilis sine cultūrā frūctuōsus esse nōn potest, sīc sine doctrīnā animus

    as a field, however fertile, cannot bear fruit without tilling, so neither can a mind without teachingCic. Tusc. 2.13

  • etenim ille, quoniam semel indūxit animum sibi licēre quod vellet, fēcisset nihilō minus mē invītō

    for once he had made up his mind that he could do as he liked, he would have done it all the same, despite meCic. Att. 14.13.6

  • Rapere est, nōn petere, quidquid invītō auferās.

    Whatever you take from someone against his will is grabbing, not asking.Publil. Sent. R 26

  • adjūrāsque id tē mē invītō nōn esse factūrum

    and you swore you would not do it without my consentCic. Phil. 2.9 (Lewis & Short)

See also however.
